name: Classical logic
quick: Logic with true-or-false propositions and elimination of double negation.
definition: In this course, a proposition and its negation cannot both hold, and denying a negation establishes the proposition. This underlies the contradiction method.
example: If assuming not S leads to $0=1$, reject not S and conclude S.
confusion: A surprising result is not an impossibility without a conflicting fact.

name: Lowest terms
quick: A fraction whose entries have no common positive divisor greater than 1.
definition: Write a rational number as a/b with integer entries, positive b, and greatest common divisor 1. Dividing by their greatest positive common divisor produces this representation.
example: $6/8$ reduces to $3/4$ by dividing both entries by 2.
confusion: Both entries being even contradicts lowest terms, not rationality by itself.

name: Greatest common divisor
quick: $\gcd(a,b)$ is the greatest positive integer dividing both entries.
definition: For integers a,b not both zero, their common positive divisors form a finite nonempty set. Its greatest member is the gcd; gcd 1 means the entries are coprime.
confusion: The gcd is a number, while a divisibility expression is a proposition.

name: Lemma
section: The irrationality of the square root of 2
quick: A proved supporting statement used in another proof.
definition: A lemma separates a useful dependency from the larger argument. It must have its own valid proof or be supplied as an established fact.
example: The fact that an even integer square has an even root supports the irrationality proof for $\sqrt2$.
confusion: Calling something a lemma does not remove the obligation to justify it.

name: Composite integer
quick: An integer greater than 1 that is not prime.
definition: A composite positive integer has a divisor strictly between 1 and itself, hence a factorization into two smaller positive integers greater than 1.
confusion: 1 is neither prime nor composite under this convention.

name: Well-ordering of integers
quick: Every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element.
definition: The property also holds for nonnegative integers and integer sets bounded below by a fixed integer. It justifies choosing the least candidate even in an infinite set.
example: A nonempty set of failing indices starting at 2 has a smallest failing index.
confusion: Positive real numbers do not have a least element.

name: Additive inverse
quick: A value that adds to the original value to make zero.
definition: An additive inverse y of x satisfies x+y=0. For real numbers it exists as -x and is unique by subtraction.
confusion: This is an inverse for addition, not an inverse function or reciprocal.

name: Discharging an assumption
section: Common errors and how to repair them
quick: End the temporary use of an assumption after its role is complete.
definition: A contradiction assumption is rejected after deriving the impossibility. It must not be reused afterward as an established fact.
example: After ruling out a greatest integer M, no subsequent argument may treat that M as existing.
confusion: Temporary assumptions have scope; a proof cannot retain a refuted premise.

name: Left inverse
section: Common errors and how to repair them
quick: A function that undoes f when applied after f.
definition: For $f:A\to B$, a left inverse $g:B\to A$ obeys $g(f(a))=a$ for every a in A. Applying g to equal f-outputs shows f is injective.
example: For $f(n)=2n$ on integers, $g(m)=\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ is a left inverse.
confusion: A left inverse need not undo f in the other order.

name: Right inverse
section: Common errors and how to repair them
quick: A function choosing an input that f sends to each target.
definition: For $f:A\to B$, a right inverse $g:B\to A$ obeys $f(g(b))=b$ for every b in B. It supplies a preimage for each target, so f is surjective.
example: For $f(x)=x^2$ from reals to nonnegative reals, $g(y)=\sqrt y$ is a right inverse.
confusion: A right inverse need not establish injectivity.
